So these are all mine now? That folder is bigger than my first year here.
Not all at once. We are phasing out my side of it over three months, and you get the template first.
All right. How much of your week did this take?
I used to spend two days a week on supply contracts. Now it is closer to half a day, and next quarter it will be none.
Two days. And the disputes? Am I taking those too?
No, the disputes stay with me. You are used to reading a contract, but you have not seen how these particular buyers behave when they stop paying.
Fair. And what is taking the two days now?
Land, permits and a thirty-year concession. Previously that work sat with an outside firm, and at the time nobody here thought we would ever do it ourselves.
Honestly, that sounds harder than what you are giving me. Is it?
It is a steep learning curve, and I am still getting used to reading technical annexes. But it is the direction the work is going, so I would rather learn it now.

Amanda, it is Karin. Quick one, and it is a good problem. The board approved the project on Tuesday, which means the environmental work stops being a side file and becomes part of your job description. So we have to decide what leaves your desk. My suggestion is this. The routine supply contracts, the ones that used to take two days a week, go to the team, with a template and a short note from you. The disputes stay with you, because nobody else has the history. And the new file grows. I know this is a steep learning curve, and I know you did not use to work with land law at all. That is also why the board wanted you and not an outside firm. Think about it and tell me on Thursday what you want to hand over and what you want to keep.

People ask me what it was like to change area after twelve years, and the honest answer has three parts. The first year was humiliating, and I mean that as a technical description, not as a complaint. I used to be the person in the room who knew the answer, and suddenly I was the person asking what a word meant. The second part is that the old knowledge does not disappear, it changes function. I do not draft the same contracts any more, but I read every new one with twelve years of disputes behind my eyes, and that is worth more here than it was where I learned it. And the third part is the one nobody tells you. You never stop feeling new, you just get used to feeling new. When that stops being uncomfortable, the move is finished.

Start with what your work used to be, before the change. Then say what happened, and when. Then say what your work is now. Then say what you are still getting used to. And finally, say what you are keeping from the old work, and why it still matters.
